messages.subject_clean: [RHadoop:#708] Using HPROF in RHadoop jobs
messages.body_plain:
Hi Rohit,
when using backend parameters you are kind of  bypassing rmr. Whatever you specify there goes onto the streaming cmd line with only simple formatting happening. Therefore I think this is a hadoop configuration issue more than an rmr issue. I tried googling the general part of the error message and you can find a few reports, mostly of the "can't write" type rather than "can't create"  but it seems to boil down to permission issues. On most hadoop installations I've seen -- not sure it's an absolute though, jobs run as a different user than your personal account, hadoop or mapred or some such. So it may be that /usr/local is not writable to that user -- it normally is writable only by root on most Unix systems I've run into. Try specifying a different path, like /tmp/hprof and see what happens. The other thing is that you can have concurrent processes trying to write to the same file -- once you solve your current problem.  This could result in corrupt hprof data. As you know, despite the H in the name, hprof is not Hadoop specific. The few examples I see online in connection with Hadoop set the filename to  %s but I don't know what that means in this context. If you know how to run a streaming job without rmr2 I would recommend straightening out the situation outside rmr2, so as to keep Hadoop issues separate from rmr2 issues. Something like

$HADOOP_CMD jar $HADOOP_STREAMING -D <your generic options here> -input <some input file> -output <some output file> -mapper cat

and get your profiling working this way. Then bring that back to rmr2. I hope this helps

Antonio

messages.subject: Trying to subset data in RMR2 for individual analysis, analogy to RHIPE
messages.subject_clean: Trying to subset data in RMR2 for individual analysis, analogy to RHIPE
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

The group behind RHIPE has a statistical approach for big data called “Divide and Recombine”.  In nutshell, you divide your data into subsets.  In a map step,  each subset becomes a value with a unique key.  In the next map step, the estimation procedure is applied to each value.  In the reduce step, the means of the estimates are taken.

I have written an algorithm for RHIPE that tests to what degree the speed of the procedure depends on the size of the subset.  The total data is a matrix with N observations and P + 1 columns, that is then split up into subsets that each have M rows, for a total of R = N/M subsets (M chosen so that R is an integer).  Assume N is a very large number.

Each of these subset then becomes a value so you have R keyvalue pairs.   So while the total amount of data N remains the same, the number of key value pairs varies, and the size of each value varies.

In the RHIPE algorithm, the data is predicted and subsetted in the first map, then glm.fit() is applied to each subset/value (P predictors and 1 response).

I am trying to write the same algorithm for RMR2, and do so in a way that the speed for RHIPE and RMR2 can be compared fairly.

The problem is creating subsets in RHIPE is easy because within a for loop, you can simulate a single subset and make it a value in a single key-value pair.  For example (R-like pseudocode, not actual RHIPE code);
map (
    for (i in 1:r) {# r is number of subsets
        mat <- (generate a matrix with m rows and p+1 columns)
        key <- i
        value <- mat
        collect(key, value) # keyvalue pairs are created iteratively
    }
)

Then in the fitting step we have;
map(
    for (i in seq_along(map.values){
        mat <- map.values[[i ]]    #iterates through all the values from last map
        coef <- glm.fit(mat)$coefficients
        key <- 1  # the same key for each subset
        value <- coef
        collect(key, value)
    }
}

Finally, these are summed up in reduce (in practice you would use mean, but sum is easier to code because its associative)
reduce(
    r <- sum(number of coefficients estimates)
    sum.coef <- sum(coefficients estimates)
    key <- 1
    value <- c(r, sum.coef)
    collect(key, value)
)

Since RMR2 doesn’t support looping, and simulating all the data at once could create problems with some data structures, I plan to read in data from the HDFS.

My question is, how should I represent subsets in RMR2?  I first tried was to simulate the data, as one big data.frame, create a factor that represents subset membership, and use the by() function to apply glm or glm.fit to the data using subset as a grouping variable.  That didn’t work because of the memory constraints of a data.frame.  I think this will work if I read in the data from the HDFS, but I am not sure if treating each row as a value as RMR2 likes to do equivalent treating subsets as values.   I also thought of creating a big list with matrix subsets as values and wrapping that with the keyval() function, then using glm.fit in lapply().  But from what I read RMR2 either doesn't support or is resistant to doing that.

Can you offer some suggestions?

Great, how would that work for the max or for quantiles? If you want to read some research on the subject, I recommend  the paper "mergeable summaries" <http://www.cs.utah.edu/~jeffp/papers/merge-summ.pdf> . Taking average of subset estimates, even babies can do that, but what are the statistical properties? You know, old fashioned bias and variance questions? If I take the average of maxes, we are just averaging the bias of each estimate. For the same computational cost, we can take the max and reduce that bias. Let's not trivialize parallel programming.

>
> I have written an algorithm for RHIPE that tests to what degree the speed of the procedure depends on the size of the subset.  The total data is a matrix with N observations and P + 1 columns, that is then split up into subsets that each have M rows, for a total of R = N/M subsets (M chosen so that R is an integer). If it's down to a speed comparison, I think you are missing the point.  rmr2 is  within 20% of java speedwise on some realistic test cases and we are working to extend that across other use cases. It's worth working on that because the resulting programs are small and elegant, no need for pseudo code to hide the boilerplate. If RHIPE has achieved Java parity speedwise, hats off but it doesn't really move the needle. There are other issues like compatibility with different distros, IO formats, it's  not just, A is faster than B, use A, drop B. Then Java or C++, if not assembly, win every time. And you wouldn't even bother building abstractions into libraries, because there is a penalty to pay, you'd rather program at the lowest level possible all the time.

> map (
>     for (i in 1:r) {# r is number of subsets
>         mat <- (generate a matrix with m rows and p+1 columns)
>         key <- i
>         value <- mat

>     }
> )
>

        coef <- glm.fit(mat)$coefficients

map =

I am not sure what your sum of coefficients does but if it is an element by element sum you can implement it as Reduce('+', vv) or as an rbind followed by a colSum, the latter should be faster.

>
> Since RMR2 doesn’t support looping,

How did this fantastic statement originate? Please don't confuse my users with these statements. rmr2 allows looping because it's just R. It uses side effects less than Rhipe because it aims to be closer to an R (functional) style than a Java style of programming.

As somebody who's spoken a non-native language for a third of my life, translating is not the right approach, you have to think in the new language. I suspect the same applies here. The rmr2 way is "very functional" so to speak and vectorized through and through. It is more memory intensive, no doubt, but I don't understand your consideration well enough to offer very precise advice. Which ones of the following is applicable

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I would like to share a plan <https://github.com/RevolutionAnalytics/RHadoop/wiki/Planning-multiple-output-feature> concerning this advanced feature. The idea is to generate two outputs with the same mapreduce job. It is completely possible to achieve the same results with multiple jobs now. This feature is only intended to save compute time. I think the main question is that if this is a feature waiting for a use case, and if any of rmr's users are so far ahead as to need this. I had one beautiful use case, stochastic SVD, but it requires a more advanced feature that can not be accessed from streaming, so it's out of reach for no (we can still implement the same algorithm, just with one or two additional jobs). So my plan is to let this sit for some time and see if any users have use cases for this feature or opinions about the proposed API. The implementation will be non-trivial, as we are trying to put some distance between the R API and the streaming API where algorithm logic is commingled with IO format issues, something we'd like to avoid in rmr. Thanks

Antonio

messages.subject: Use of stdin and stdout in map and reduce functions
messages.subject_clean: Use of stdin and stdout in map and reduce functions
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
it has come to my attention that the issue of using IO streams inside the map and reduce functions is creating some trouble. Let me try to clarify.

Specifcations
Stdin and stdout are reserved to communication between R and hadoop, therefore code in the map and reduce functions can not access them. This has always been the case but will be documented in the manual for the mapreduce function in the next relesase
Stderr (where warnings and calls to message go by default in case you wonder what that is) is redirected by hadoop to console in standalone mode and the appropriate log file in all other modes (accessible through the jobtracker web interface). There are no changes concerning this either but for better documentation.
Implementation changes

In previous versions calls to the map and reduce functions were surrounded with sink calls so as to prevent them from writing to stdout. This was not completely effective as there are many different ways to write to stdout in R, some of which are not affected by sink calls. Also, it had a serious performance cost in some instances. It was never documented but some users relied on this and now find that their code breaks on upgrading to 2.1.0, where these calls were removed.

Symptoms

The errors reported are completely random and uninformative, we've seen out of memory errors in the Java parsing code, SIGPIPE signals, you name it. You need to be alert to this issue.

Solutions

The solution is to "silence" your map and reduce code, writing any logging and diagnostic messages to stderr (using rmr.str or message for instance). For library functions, you can try to turn off logging (options such as debug or trace are usually related to this behavior, but this changes package by package) or surround them with a sink(stderr()) and a sink(NULL) pair of calls. Sometimes sink doesn't work: in this case my suggestion is to reach out to the library developer and submit a ticket. Messages out to be written to stderr as a matter of correct design, at least in the Unix tradition, and some package developers are responsive to this and have fixed their packages. Notably, the R core developers do not believe this is an issue, so we will have to deal with it for the foreseeable future. Thanks

Antonio

Doesn't happen to me, so we need to have some code here to make the discussion concrete.

from.dfs(mapreduce(to.dfs(1:10), map = function(k,v) if(sum(v) < 15) keyval(1,v), reduce = function(k,vv) sum(vv)))

Of course this would go though in a single map call at defaults or any reasonable setting, so I set

rmr.options(keyval.length=2)

beforehand. That makes rmr call the map function twice on this example. The second time the map function returns NULL. It works just fine. What you may be doing is mixing keyval(1,10) and keyval(NULL, 10). That is something I decided to disallow when it tightened the semantics for keyval related operations following some bug reports and requests for clarfication. The idea is that you need to be able to do recycling of keyval args to bring them to the same lenght (or nrow if matrix or data frame). When you have 0-length and non-0-length there is no amount of recycling that will achieve that. An exception is cut for to.dfs or map only job. When all the keys are NULL it is understood as keys missing. If there is a reduce phase, we need keys to guide the grouping, so this is disallowed. If there is a mix of keyval pairs, some with keys and some without, even without reduce, I couldn't come up with any meaningful definition that was consistent with the rest, but it may be just me. Imagine that keyval is just a cbind with a special role for some columns and that when you call map multiple times you need to apply a rbind to keys and values, after recycling of arguments, to make them into a single data structure (that doesn't always happen, but the idea is that it should always be possible, either in the preparation to the reduce call or in a from.dfs call). If you call cbind (NULL, mtcars) it fails but let's say we relaxed it to return mtcars;  then you call cbind(1, mtcars) and it will add a column if 1s. Then you try to rbind them and it will fail because of the discrepancy in the number of columns. We could switch to a semantics inspired by rbind.fill and see where that leads us (match same name cols, add all the other cols, fill in with NAs. In fact, we are already using rbind.fill behind the scenes to support outer joins.

> If I use 0-length keyval for the records I want to drop, I don't get an error message, but for the records I do want to keep, there is a problem. In particular, for the records I do want to keep, I use return(keyval(x, y)), where y is a 1 by 2 matrix. However, while rmr keeps the first column of that matrix, it drops the second column of that matrix, although I would like to keep that column.

> The "normal case" does work, where I use return(keyval(NA, y)) for the records I want to discard, and return(keyval(x, y)) for the records I want to keep.

That is not filtering, you can do it, but it doesn't discard any records unless you later check for NA and discard them. I would call it a workaround at best.
